patient.chief_complaint: Prolonged unresponsiveness, rhythmic extremity movements — EEG team disagrees whether this is NCSE or psychogenic non-epileptic status
patient.history_present_illness: A 38-year-old Hispanic female nurse was brought to the emergency department by her colleague after prolonged unresponsive episodes at their hospital unit. The patient had been at work when she suddenly became unresponsive and collapsed. Her colleague reported that she appeared to have rhythmic shaking of both arms for several minutes, then appeared to 'wake up' briefly, then became unresponsive again with more subtle rhythmic movements of the legs. Total duration of apparent seizure-like activity was over 30 minutes before EMS arrived. She has a known diagnosis of epilepsy diagnosed 8 years ago with generalized tonic-clonic seizures, now well-controlled on lamotrigine for the past 3 years without a breakthrough seizure. The colleague noted she had been under extreme stress recently — her mother was hospitalized with cancer last week, and she had been working 12-hour night shifts. The colleague is also aware the patient has a history of psychogenic non-epileptic seizures (PNES), diagnosed 2 years ago after video-EEG monitoring, and has been in therapy. The patient is known to have both true epilepsy and PNES — a common and diagnostically challenging combination. On EMS arrival, she was unresponsive with eyes closed, making occasional moaning sounds. On ED arrival, 35 minutes after onset, she continues with intermittent bilateral arm trembling with eyes closed. She is not responding to commands. EMG artifact and motion artifact make initial EEG interpretation extremely challenging. Lamotrigine level drawn on arrival.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Appears unresponsive with eyes closed. Intermittent moaning. When examiner attempts to open eyelids, patient actively closes eyes — 'active eye closure' sign. Occasional purposeful-appearing arm movements inconsistent with epileptic activity.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, equal and reactive. No oculomotor palsy. No corneal reflex abnormality. Eyes actively close when opened by examiner.
neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral rhythmic arm trembling that waxes and wanes. Movements irregular in amplitude and frequency. No sustained tonic posturing. No Jacksonian march.
neurological_exam.sensory: Appears not to respond to noxious stimuli, but withdrawal inconsistent with true unconsciousness.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ throughout. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Babinski.
neurological_exam.additional: Semiological features: eyes closed throughout, active eye closure when opened, waxing-waning intensity of movements, pelvic thrusting noted intermittently, head turning side to side. No post-ictal confusion period after movements resolve.

background.dominant_rhythm: 9-10 Hz posterior dominant rhythm bilaterally — normal for age
background.organization: well-organized posterior dominant rhythm; normal anterior-posterior gradient

eeg.impression: This is a NORMAL EEG. Normal 9-10 Hz posterior dominant rhythm bilaterally; no focal slowing; no epileptiform discharges; no electrographic seizures recorded. The posterior dominant rhythm was persistently present during clinical shaking episodes recorded on this study. Extensive motion/EMG artifact during clinical events significantly limits interpretation and cannot be excluded as a source of false-negative results. Video-EEG with improved artifact control is recommended for definitive characterization of events
eeg.limitations: Extensive motion artifact during clinical events. Initial recording performed without video monitoring.
recommended_actions: Video-EEG monitoring recommended for definitive event characterization.

Toxicology.value: Negative for cocaine, amphetamines, benzodiazepines, PCP, opioids

Post-ictal markers.reference_range: 2-29 baseline; >200% baseline expected post-generalized seizure within 20-60 min

ct.impression: Normal non-contrast CT head. No acute intracranial hemorrhage, mass lesion, or structural abnormality

background.dominant_rhythm: 9-10 Hz normal posterior dominant rhythm persistently present even during clinical shaking events

output.impression: This is a NORMAL EEG. Normal 9-10 Hz posterior dominant rhythm was persistently present during all 3 clinical events captured on simultaneous video-EEG. No epileptiform discharges, no focal slowing, no ictal discharges, no post-ictal suppression were recorded during or between events. No electrographic seizures were recorded. A normal EEG during captured clinical events, with preservation of posterior dominant rhythm, is not consistent with generalized convulsive or non-convulsive electrographic seizure activity at those times
output.limitations: Some residual EMG artifact during peak movement phases.

results.title: Treatment of psychogenic nonepileptic seizures
results.key_finding: Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) is the only evidence-based treatment for PNES with Level A recommendation. Communicating diagnosis clearly and compassionately is essential. Benzodiazepine use for presumed SE in PNES patients is a common harmful error — may reinforce behavior, cause respiratory depression, and delay appropriate psychiatric treatment. Video-EEG is the gold standard diagnostic test.

results.title: Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures in patients with comorbid epilepsy
results.key_finding: 20-40% of PNES patients have coexisting epilepsy. Lamotrigine appropriate for JME. PNES events must be distinguished from epileptic events using video-EEG. Key distinguishing features of PNES: eyes closed during events, active eye-closure, normal EEG during events, normal prolactin post-event, waxing-waning symptom intensity, pelvic thrusting, side-to-side head shaking.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
DaTscan / dopamine transporter imaging has no role in SE; no parkinsonism question relevant to acute management.
No infectious or autoimmune signs; LP not indicated.

sequence_constraints.reason: EEG must precede further AED escalation when PNES is on the differential.

critical_actions: Continuous video-EEG with semiology capture is THE diagnostic test
Single dose of IV lorazepam is reasonable initial; do NOT escalate to intubation/anesthetic before EEG confirms epileptic SE
Once PNES confirmed, gentle communication of diagnosis and CBT referral
Continue therapeutic AED for comorbid JME
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT intubate or initiate anesthetic infusions for PNES — iatrogenic harm
Do NOT escalate AEDs aggressively before EEG confirms epileptic pattern
Do NOT dismiss the patient — PNES is a real disorder requiring treatment
Escalating AED loading and intubation for confirmed PNES exposes the patient to iatrogenic harm without benefit — once EEG confirms PNES, de-escalate.
key_reasoning_points: Video-EEG is the gold standard for distinguishing PNES from epileptic SE
Serial prolactin (15-20 min post-event) often elevated after epileptic GTC but not PNES
Normal lactate post-event argues strongly against epileptic SE
PNES treatment is CBT — AED escalation is harmful and counterproductive
Patients can have BOTH epilepsy and PNES (this patient has known JME + PNES)
